title: How Wills Work
summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about favorite 1979 movies and the 1980s comedy Scavenger Hunt, then turn to how wills work. They cover the basics of a valid will (name, spouse, children, executor and alternate, debts, burial wishes, retirement and insurance beneficiaries, age 18 and sound mind), the difference between wills and beneficiary designations, and types of wills: oral, deathbed, holographic, DIY/self-proving, and ironclad. They discuss changing wills via codicils, grounds for challenging a will, disinheriting children versus spouses (in terrorem clauses), estate or "death" taxes, trusts, living wills and power of attorney. They close with odd will stories and a listener mail request from Timmy about his breakup with Elaine.

segments.title: Opening banter and Scavenger Hunt
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck trade favorite 1979 movies and Josh recommends the Vincent Price comedy Scavenger Hunt, using its will-based plot as a lead-in to the topic.

segments.title: Will basics and legal disclaimer
segments.summary: The hosts note they are not attorneys and that state law governs wills. They say DIY will forms are available cheaply, but an attorney should review the document. Wills can be valid across states, though checking local law is advised.

segments.title: Essential contents of a will
segments.summary: Key elements include the testator's name, spouse and marriage date, children's names, treatment of stepchildren, revocation of prior wills, executor and alternate, powers, gifts, debt instructions and distribution. Burial wishes belong elsewhere, and retirement plans, life insurance and annuities pass by beneficiary designation rather than by will.

segments.title: Eligibility: age and sound mind
segments.summary: A testator generally must be 18 and of sound mind, meaning they know their property and are not suffering from mental illness. Mental illness that begins after the will is written does not invalidate it. Wills should not be drafted under the influence of people urging burning of documents.

segments.title: Choosing an executor
segments.summary: The executor inventories assets, pays legitimate debts, and distributes assets under the will. The hosts advise picking someone trustworthy, organized, with business sense and good bedside manner.

segments.title: Types of wills: oral, deathbed, holographic, DIY, ironclad
segments.summary: Oral wills are spoken before witnesses, often by dying soldiers, and are upheld when witnesses agree. Deathbed wills are a time-based category often challenged for capacity. Holographic wills are handwritten and not recognized in all states. DIY and self-proving wills save time, and ironclad wills are lawyer-drafted with witness affidavits that avoid probate testimony.

segments.title: Changing and challenging a will
segments.summary: Only the testator can change a will, using a new will or a codicil. Reasons to change include marriage, divorce, children, or tax changes. Challenging a will requires legal standing, such as being named in the will or a blood or marriage relative, and grounds like a missing witness, coercion, fraud, or an improperly named executor. Wills are rarely overturned, and rejected wills default to intestate state law.

segments.title: Disinheriting children and spouses
segments.summary: Children can be disinherited with a clear statement, while disinheriting a spouse is harder and often requires a prenuptial agreement or leaving a modest bequest with an in terrorem clause that forfeits gifts if the will is challenged.

segments.title: Estate tax and death tax
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the so-called death tax is an estate tax levied on beneficiaries' bequests, with a 2006 example of tax on a $10,050 inheritance. They discuss loopholes favoring the wealthy and how trusts can reduce taxes, keep assets out of probate, and manage money for minors.

segments.title: Living wills and power of attorney
segments.summary: A living will covers medical decisions such as life support rather than property, and is usually paired with a power of attorney that names who makes decisions if the person cannot.

segments.title: Unusual will stories
segments.summary: The hosts recount odd bequests: a Portuguese aristocrat who left money to 70 strangers, an unsuccessful composer's opera offer to the Met, a businessman who left Nokia shares to rest home friends, Ed Headrick's frisbee ashes plan, Mark Gruenwald's ashes in a comic, Dusty Springfield's cat provision, Leona Helmsley's dog bequest, and a tree in Athens that owns itself.

segments.title: Listener mail: Timmy and Elaine
segments.summary: A listener named Timmy asks the hosts to encourage his ex-girlfriend Elaine to get back together with him after an eighteen-month relationship ended amicably. Chuck declines to make more such requests.

segments.title: Sign-off and listener call for stories
segments.summary: The hosts ask listeners to send crazy will stories via Facebook, Twitter, or email, point to the How Stuff Works article on wills, and sign off.
